title: The ops "scrape success rate < 50%" alert can never fire: the payload it is handed never carries the key, and /api/status carries it as a dict the float() cast rejects
claimUnderTest: src/api/ops_alerts.py's module docstring: "Fires SMTP emails ... when any of these conditions hold: * Scrape success rate over the last 24h drops below 50%".
observed: server.py:11748 calls _scrape_status_payload() and passes it as status_payload. _scrape_status_payload() returns dict(scrape_status) plus exactly three keys (stall_threshold_sec, run_timeout_sec, status_summary). An AST scan of every write into the scrape_status global finds 23 keys; scrape_success_rate_24h is not one of them. _check_scrape_rate therefore gets None from .get() and returns None on line 48 on every sweep. Separately, the key DOES exist on /api/status (added at server.py:4352 inside get_status, a different function) but its value is the DICT {"total","success","failure","rate"} returned by _scrape_success_rate_24h(), so even if the payloads were swapped, float(dict) raises TypeError which line 51-52 swallows into another None. Both routes to the alert are closed. Nothing else in the repo reads scrape_success_rate_24h except tests/api/test_ops_alerts.py, which feeds a bare float that no production caller produces — the test passes and the alert is still dead.

reproduction.command: .venv/bin/python -c "import sys; sys.path.insert(0,'.'); from src.api.ops_alerts import _check_scrape_rate; print('status_payload shape:', _check_scrape_rate({'running':False,'stalled':False})); print('/api/status shape:', _check_scrape_rate({'scrape_success_rate_24h':{'total':10,'success':1,'failure':9,'rate':0.1}})); print('test-only shape:', _check_scrape_rate({'scrape_success_rate_24h':0.1}))"
reproduction.expected: An OpsAlert for the 10%-success case in at least one of the two production shapes
reproduction.actual: status_payload shape: None / /api/status shape: None / test-only shape: OpsAlert(severity='critical', ...) — only the shape no caller produces alerts

numericProof.formula: fire iff float(status_payload['scrape_success_rate_24h']) < 0.5; both production shapes short-circuit to None before the comparison

userImpact: No user-facing wrong number, but the operator is not told when more than half the scheduled scrapes fail. The board silently ages while every alert channel stays quiet, so the first signal is a user noticing stale values.

priorFinding.note: Independently reproduced and extended: the prior finding named only the missing key. The second, independent kill — /api/status carries the key as a dict, so float() raises and the except swallows it — means fixing the wiring alone would not revive the alert.

whatWorks: The other three ops checks (_check_circuit_breakers, _check_contract_health, _check_data_freshness) receive real inputs from server.py:11755-11762 and can fire. The 4h cooldown and recovery-alert machinery are exercised by tests and are sound.
rootCause: Two functions named similarly: _scrape_status_payload() (the alert's input, built from the scrape_status global) and get_status() (the HTTP handler, which decorates that payload with derived fields). The alert was written against the HTTP response shape and wired to the internal one, and the derived field is a dict rather than the scalar the checker expects.
requiredRepair: In server.py:11748 pass {**_scrape_status_payload(), 'scrape_success_rate_24h': _scrape_success_rate_24h().get('rate')} (or have _check_scrape_rate accept the dict and read ['rate']). Add a test that feeds the actual production payload, not a hand-built float.

title: A partial scrape that the promotion guard REFUSES to publish is recorded as a success — same event name, same history outcome, same last_success_at, and it increments scrape_count
claimUnderTest: server.py:2362 comment — "R-3: Block partial scrape promotion — don't overwrite good data with degraded data". The implied contract is that a blocked run is visibly not a good run.
observed: On the blocked branch server.py:2380 calls _mark_scrape_success(elapsed, player_count, site_count, total_sites) before returning the OLD data. _mark_scrape_success sets last_success_at and last_scrape to now, clears error to None, sets current_step='complete', increments scrape_count, emits the event scrape_succeeded, and appends outcome='success' to scrape_history. The only distinguishing artifact is a second run_event 'partial_scrape_blocked' at warning level emitted immediately afterward. Every aggregate built on scrape_history or last_success_at — _scrape_success_rate_24h(), /api/health's last_scrape, /api/metrics' scrape_total — counts the blocked run as a clean success. Compounded by W23-F003: the guard only trips on total data loss, so reaching this branch at all means the scrape returned literally zero sites, which is the single worst outcome and it is filed as a success.

reproduction.actual: _mark_scrape_success(...) then `return latest_data` — line 2380 followed by line 2388

numericProof.formula: success_rate_24h = successes/total over scrape_history; a blocked run contributes +1 to BOTH numerator and denominator

userImpact: An operator looking at /admin or /api/health after a total scrape failure sees a fresh timestamp, no error, and a 100% success rate. They conclude the pipeline is healthy and do not investigate, while the site serves last-known-good data indefinitely.

priorFinding.note: Reproduced by reading the live code path. Adds the specific downstream consumers that inherit the lie (scrape_history outcome, last_success_at, scrape_count, /api/metrics.scrape_total) and the interaction with W23-F003.

whatWorks: The guard itself does the right thing with the DATA — it returns latest_data and does not overwrite the good snapshot on disk or in memory. send_alert() is also called on this branch, so an email does go out if SMTP is configured. The defect is purely in the status/history bookkeeping.
rootCause: The blocked branch needs to clear the 'running' flag and stamp a finish time, and _mark_scrape_success is the only helper that does that — so it was reused for its side effects rather than its meaning.
requiredRepair: Split the bookkeeping: a _mark_scrape_finished(outcome) that both success and blocked-partial call, with outcome='partial_blocked' recorded to scrape_history and last_success_at left untouched on the blocked path.
dependencies: W23-F003 (same branch); W23-F001 (the success-rate metric this corrupts is itself unread)

title: The "fewer than half the sites returned" partial-scrape guard degenerates to "block only on total loss": `sites` carries 2 entries on the live snapshot and only lists sources that already produced values
claimUnderTest: server.py:2362-2363 — "Block partial scrape promotion — don't overwrite good data with degraded data when fewer than half the sites returned results."
observed: site_count counts entries of result['sites'] with playerCount>0; total_sites is len(result['sites']). On the live snapshot data/dynasty_data_2026-08-04.json, `sites` is a LIST of exactly 2 dicts — [{'key':'ktc',...,'playerCount':500},{'key':'idpTradeCalc',...,'playerCount':900}] — so the test is `site_count < 1.0`, i.e. it fires only when ZERO sites returned data. Worse, sites_meta is built by iterating `active_sites` (Dynasty Scraper.py:5413), the sources that actually ran, so a source that is skipped shrinks the denominator with the numerator: the two sources that DID fail this run (KTC_TradeDB, KTC_WaiverDB, both 'partial' per settings.sourceRunSummary) are absent from `sites` entirely. Meanwhile the served board blends 21 sources (/api/status.served_source_coverage), none of the other 19 of which the guard can see at all. The guard cannot distinguish 'KTC returned 500 rows and IDPTC returned 900' from 'KTC returned 1 row and IDPTC returned 1 row'.

reproduction.command: .venv/bin/python -c "import json; d=json.load(open('data/dynasty_data_2026-08-04.json')); s=d['sites']; sc=len([x for x in s if x.get('playerCount',0)>0]); print('type',type(s).__name__,'total_sites',len(s),'site_count',sc,'threshold',len(s)/2,'blocks?',sc<len(s)/2); print('served sources:',len(json.load(open('docs/master-site-audit/evidence/W23/api-status.json'))['served_source_coverage']))"
reproduction.expected: A guard whose denominator is the ~21 sources the board actually blends
reproduction.actual: type list total_sites 2 site_count 2 threshold 1.0 blocks? False — and served sources: 21

numericProof.formula: block iff site_count < total_sites/2  =>  site_count < 1.0  =>  block iff site_count == 0

userImpact: A scrape in which 20 of 21 sources collapse promotes cleanly to production. Every value on /rankings, /trade and /draft is then a near-single-source blend presented with the same confidence chrome as a full 21-source consensus, and the single-source haircut is the only thing standing between the user and a one-vendor board.

priorFinding.note: Confirmed with one correction: `sites` is a LIST, not a dict as the prior finding says — the arithmetic and the conclusion are unaffected. Extended with the second, worse property the prior finding missed: sites_meta is derived from active_sites, so failed/skipped sources leave the denominator rather than zeroing the numerator, and 19 of the 21 blended sources are structurally invisible to the guard.

whatWorks: The guard's intent and its data handling are correct — on a true total loss it does refuse to promote and does return the previous snapshot. `served_source_coverage` (server.py:4350) already computes the honest 21-source count and its own comment admits `source_health` "cannot detect a degraded board".
rootCause: `sites` is legacy scraper metadata describing the browser-driven sources only; the modern pipeline gets 19 of its 21 sources from scripts/fetch_*.py CSVs that never enter sites_meta. The guard was written against the legacy structure and never re-pointed.
requiredRepair: Gate on served_source_coverage (or on settings.sourceRunSummary.enabledSources vs completeSources) rather than on `sites`. Compare against the previous snapshot's per-source coverage so a source dropping from 400 rows to 3 also trips the guard.

title: verify-sharp-production.yml runs on EVERY push to main and always fails at `git add data/ops/...` because .gitignore excludes data/ — so its "Enforce healthy population" verdict step has never once executed
claimUnderTest: The workflow's final step, "Enforce healthy population", is supposed to raise SystemExit when the Sharp production smoke is not healthy — i.e. this is the gate that makes a broken Sharp deploy go red.
observed: The preceding step runs `git add data/ops/sharp-production-smoke.json`. `.gitignore:45` is a bare `data/` and only `data/ros/` is re-included, so that path is ignored. git refuses an explicitly-named ignored pathspec with exit 1, and GitHub Actions' default shell is `bash -e {0}`, so the step dies on that line — the `git commit` after it never runs and the verdict step, which carries the default `if: success()`, is skipped. `git log --all -- data/ops/` returns nothing: the directory has never been committed in the repo's history, which is what a permanently-failing add looks like from the outside. The workflow's `on:` is `push: branches:[main]` with `paths-ignore: [data/**, exports/**]` plus `workflow_run` after Deploy Production, so this fires on essentially every code push. Its wait loop is `for attempt in range(1,81)` with `time.sleep(30)` on each miss = 2,400 s = 40 minutes of billed runner time per push, under a 50-minute job timeout, ending in a red X that says nothing about Sharp's actual health. The other three Sharp diagnostic workflows share the identical `git add` bug, but they lose only their artifact (their commit step is last and is `if: always()`), and none of them runs on an unfiltered push to main — force-sharp-production-now, trigger-sharp-now-via-merge and trigger-sharp-no-environment all filter `paths:` to their own workflow file.

reproduction.command: bash docs/master-site-audit/evidence/W23/gitignore-repro.sh; git check-ignore -v data/ops/sharp-production-smoke.json; git log --all --oneline -- data/ops/ | wc -l
reproduction.expected: REACHED: git commit printed, step exit 0, data/ops/ present in history
reproduction.actual: "The following paths are ignored by one of your .gitignore files: data" / STEP EXIT=1 / .gitignore:45:data/ / 0 commits ever touched data/ops/

numericProof.formula: worst-case wait = attempts × sleep = 80 × 30 s = 2400 s = 40 min; verdict steps executed = 0 because the preceding step exits 1 under bash -e

userImpact: No direct user-facing number. The consequence is that the ONE automated check on whether the Sharp cohort actually populated in production has never run, so /market/sharp-tracker can serve an empty or cohort_building board indefinitely with CI showing a failure that everyone has learned to read as "the flaky sharp job again".

priorFinding.note: The git-add-a-gitignored-path mechanism is CONFIRMED for all four workflows (also matches PRIOR-A16-F06). Two parts of the prior claim are REFUTED by the trigger blocks: only verify-sharp-production.yml runs on every push to main (the other three filter `paths:` to their own file and effectively never fire), and only verify-sharp-production.yml loses a downstream verdict step — the other three put their commit last under `if: always()`, so they lose an artifact, not a gate. The 40-minute figure is confirmed but applies to that one workflow (the other three cap at 120/30/20 min).

whatWorks: scheduled-refresh.yml and weekly-narratives.yml commit generated data correctly by using `git add -f` / explicit negation, so the repo already contains the working pattern. The smoke's polling logic and its healthy criteria (sleeper_started AND ffpc_started) are reasonable.
rootCause: The four workflows were written to persist a diagnostic under data/ops/ without noticing that `data/` is gitignored wholesale, and none of them used the `-f` that the repo's other data-committing workflows use.
requiredRepair: Either `git add -f data/ops/<file>` in all four, or (better for verify-sharp-production) drop the commit step entirely and move the verdict directly after the poll — a per-push smoke result does not need to be in git, and `actions/upload-artifact` already covers it. Also reconsider the every-push trigger: 40 minutes of runner per code push for a production-state probe belongs on a schedule.

title: The Sharp production smoke reports `unmappedAssets` from `dataQuality`, a key /api/sharp/market has never emitted — it is hard-zero on every run
claimUnderTest: The smoke payload's ffpcMarket.unmappedAssets is supposed to surface how many FFPC assets failed identity mapping, so an ingestion regression is visible in the recorded result.
observed: The workflow reads `(market.get("dataQuality") or {}).get("unmappedAssets", 0)`. src/sharp/market.py:410-413 emits the value under `coverage.unmappedAssets`, and the live payload has no `dataQuality` key at any level. The `or {}` plus the `, 0` default means the miss is indistinguishable from a genuine zero, so the field reads as a clean bill of health forever.

reproduction.command: curl -s -b /tmp/audit-cookies-w23.txt http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/sharp/market | .venv/bin/python -c "import json,sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print('top-level keys:', list(d.keys())); print('has dataQuality:', 'dataQuality' in d); print('coverage keys:', list(d['coverage'].keys()))"
reproduction.actual: top-level keys: ['status','generatedAt','methodologyVersion','query','assets','cohort','coverage','formula'] / has dataQuality: False / coverage keys: ['platforms','unmappedAssets']

numericProof.formula: reported = payload.get('dataQuality',{}).get('unmappedAssets',0); the key is absent so reported == 0 for all inputs

userImpact: Nobody acts on this directly — but an FFPC identity-mapping collapse would leave the recorded smoke saying zero unmapped assets, so the one artifact an operator would consult after a Sharp regression actively misdirects them.

priorFinding.note: Confirmed at runtime against the live /api/sharp/market payload rather than by reading code; the emitting site (src/sharp/market.py:413, under `coverage`) is named so the fix is a one-word change.

whatWorks: The sibling reads in the same block — coverage.platforms.ffpc.transactions/.movements, cohort.*, len(assets) — all hit real keys and would report real numbers.
rootCause: The workflow was written against a payload shape that either predates or was never shipped by src/sharp/market.py, and `.get(..., 0)` hides the mismatch.
requiredRepair: Change to `(market.get("coverage") or {}).get("unmappedAssets")` and drop the 0 default so an absent key records null, not a health claim.
dependencies: W23-F004 (same workflow; the step this feeds never commits anyway)

title: /api/metrics.data_age_seconds and /api/health.data_age_hours measure time since the process loaded the file, not since the data was scraped — they are numerically identical to uptime and reset to zero on every restart
claimUnderTest: frontend/components/StaleDataBanner.jsx:10 — "``data_age_hours`` — hours since the last successful scrape", and server.py:4508 — "R-1: Data freshness check — flag stale if no refresh in SCRAPE_INTERVAL_HOURS * 3".
observed: Both fields derive from latest_data_source['loadedAt'], which _set_latest_data_source (server.py:1307-1315) sets to _utc_now_iso() — the wall-clock moment this process read the file — regardless of when the data inside it was produced. On a disk-cache load at boot that is server start time, so data age and uptime are the same number. Measured live: uptime_seconds 7401 and data_age_seconds 7401, byte-identical, while the snapshot's own settings.sourceRunSummary.finishedAt is 2026-08-04T18:20:04Z, making the true age 14,117 s. The staleness threshold is SCRAPE_INTERVAL_HOURS*3 = 6 h, so data would have to be 6 h older than the last RESTART to trip — a server that restarts on any cadence under 6 h can never report stale data, however old it is. The same loadedAt feeds ops_alerts._check_data_freshness at server.py:11749-11754, so the operator email inherits the identical blind spot. The correct timestamps exist and are already served three feet away: /api/status.source_health.sources[*].ageHours reports the honest 3.83 h per source.

reproduction.command: curl -s -b /tmp/audit-cookies-w23.txt http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/metrics | .venv/bin/python -c "import json,sys,datetime; m=json.load(sys.stdin); scrape=datetime.datetime.fromisoformat('2026-08-04T18:20:04.195690+00:00'); true_age=(datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc)-scrape).total_seconds(); print('data_age_seconds',m['data_age_seconds'],'uptime_seconds',m['uptime_seconds'],'equal?',m['data_age_seconds']==m['uptime_seconds']); print('true age from sourceRunSummary.finishedAt', round(true_age), 'under-report h', round((true_age-m['data_age_seconds'])/3600,2)); print('data_stale',m['data_stale'])"
reproduction.actual: data_age_seconds 7401 uptime_seconds 7401 equal? True / true age 14117 / under-report 1.87 h / data_stale False

numericProof.formula: reported_age = now - loadedAt (= now - server_start on a cache load); true_age = now - sourceRunSummary.finishedAt; error = server_start - scrape_finished

userImpact: A user on /rankings trades off values that are hours older than the page admits: StaleDataBanner reads data_age_hours and stays silent, so a board that has not refreshed since a scraper outage looks current the moment the service is restarted — and restarting is exactly what an operator does when a scrape hangs. The staleness warning is suppressed by the very action taken in response to staleness.

priorFinding.note: Not in the prior index. PRIOR-A06-F11 concerns /settings' 'Live' badge measuring contract presence rather than freshness; this is the sibling defect one layer down, in the number that badge's honest counterpart is supposed to use.

whatWorks: /api/status.source_health.sources[*].lastFetched/ageHours are computed from real per-source fetch stamps and were correct on the live payload (3.83 h, matching the snapshot). SourceHealthStrip already prefers those per-source ages. The fix has a correct source of truth to point at.
rootCause: latest_data_source['loadedAt'] conflates 'when this process obtained the data' with 'when the data was made'. That is the right semantic for the disk_cache/scrape_run provenance field it was built for, and the wrong one for freshness, but it is the only timestamp the health path reaches for.
requiredRepair: Derive age from the payload's own settings.sourceRunSummary.finishedAt (falling back to scrapeTimestamp / date) in both /api/health and /api/metrics and in the ops_alerts call site, and keep loadedAt as provenance only. Assert in a test that data_age != uptime for a cache-loaded snapshot.
dependencies: W23-F001 (the ops alert that consumes the same wrong number is itself half-dead)

title: /tools/source-health claims "Scraper status for every ranking source in the pipeline" and renders 4 sources; the live board blends 21
claimUnderTest: The page's own subtitle: "Scraper status for every ranking source in the pipeline."
observed: SourceHealthStrip builds its row set from `runtime.enabled_sources` (status.source_health.source_runtime.enabled_sources) — the legacy browser-driven scraper's source list, today ['IDPTradeCalc','KTC','KTC_TradeDB','KTC_WaiverDB']. The live board blends 21 sources per /api/status.served_source_coverage, and /api/status.source_health.sources already carries per-source freshness for 22 of them. The 17 sources rendered nowhere on this page include every rank-signal contributor: dlfSf, dlfIdp, dlfRookieSf, dlfRookieIdp, idpShow, fantasyCalc, dynastyDaddySf, dynastyNerdsSfTep, yahooBoone, fantasyProsSf, fantasyProsIdp, fantasyProsFitzmaurice, flockFantasySf, flockFantasySfRookies, draftSharks, draftSharksIdp, otcffbSf, pfkDynasty, fantasyNavigatorSf. Verified in a real browser with the protocol's request-interception topology: the page header reads "Sources · 4 · 4h ago · 2 issues". The exact failure mode source_health_alerts.py was written for per CLAUDE.md — "IDP Show prod cookie expired and the source went silently stale for two weeks" — is invisible on the only page dedicated to source health.

reproduction.command: curl -s -b /tmp/audit-cookies-w23.txt http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/status | .venv/bin/python -c "import json,sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin); en=d['source_health']['source_runtime']['enabled_sources']; print('rendered by SourceHealthStrip:', len(en), en); print('served by the board:', len(d['served_source_coverage'])); print('freshness stamps available:', len(d['source_health']['sources'])); print('invisible:', sorted(set(d['served_source_coverage']) - set(en)))"
reproduction.actual: rendered 4 ['IDPTradeCalc','KTC','KTC_TradeDB','KTC_WaiverDB'] / served 21 / freshness stamps available 22 / 21 invisible — browser confirms header "Sources · 4"

userImpact: An operator (or a user who navigates to /tools/source-health after noticing odd values) reads "Sources · 4 · 2 issues", concludes the two flagged KTC sub-feeds are the whole story, and does not discover that e.g. idpShow has been stale for a fortnight — because that source has no row on the page at all.

priorFinding.note: The prior finding notes /settings' 'Live' badge contradicts /tools/source-health for the same source. That contradiction is real but the deeper problem is on the /tools/source-health side: it only knows about 4 of 21 sources, so for 17 sources there is nothing to contradict. New in this shard: the 19-source list and the browser-verified 'Sources · 4' header.

whatWorks: For the four sources it does render, the component is good: it prefers the per-source ageHours over the aggregate, surfaces source_failures[].details.message inline, and (per its own comment) deliberately renders an explicit failure state on the page variant rather than hiding. server.py:4350 already computes and serves the honest 21-source served_source_coverage — the correct input exists and is unused by this component.
rootCause: enabled_sources describes the Playwright scraper's run plan, which stopped being the whole ingestion story when 19 sources moved to scripts/fetch_*.py CSVs. The component was pointed at the run plan rather than at the board.
requiredRepair: Render the union of served_source_coverage keys and source_health.sources keys, using source_runtime only to annotate which of them the scraper drives. Retire enabled_sources as the row set.
dependencies: W23-F008, W23-F003 (all three descend from the legacy 2-to-4-source view of ingestion)

title: /api/status.source_health reports total_sources 2, sources_with_data 2, missing_sources [] for a board built from 21 sources — a 19-source outage would still read as 2 of 2 with nothing missing
claimUnderTest: The field names themselves: total_sources / sources_with_data / missing_sources on /api/status.source_health assert a complete accounting of the board's inputs.
observed: source_health is derived from the legacy `sites` array (2 entries on the live snapshot) rather than from the board. The live payload reports total_sources 2, sources_with_data 2, source_counts {ktc:500, idpTradeCalc:900}, missing_sources []. The same response's served_source_coverage lists 21 sources with real per-source row counts, and source_health.sources carries 22 freshness stamps — so the honest numbers are present in the SAME payload, two keys away. server.py's own comment at 4347-4349 concedes the point: "``source_health`` above is derived from the 3-source legacy ``sites`` list and cannot detect a degraded board." (Note the comment says 3; the live value is 2.) missing_sources is empty by construction because the denominator is whatever ran, so it can never name a source that failed to run at all.

reproduction.command: curl -s -b /tmp/audit-cookies-w23.txt http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/status | .venv/bin/python -c "import json,sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin); sh=d['source_health']; print('total_sources',sh['total_sources'],'with_data',sh['sources_with_data'],'missing',sh['missing_sources']); print('served_source_coverage n =',len(d['served_source_coverage']))"
reproduction.expected: total_sources 21, missing_sources naming any of the 21 that produced no rows

userImpact: Indirect but systemic: this is the field any external monitor, dashboard or on-call check would naturally alert on, and it is green in every degradation short of the scraper itself failing to start.

priorFinding.note: Not in the prior index as its own entry; it is the shared root cause behind PRIOR-A07-F02 (confirmed here as W23-F003) and the /tools/source-health gap (W23-F007). Recorded separately because the fix is different: the guard needs a new denominator, the page needs a new row set, and this field needs to be either recomputed or deleted.

whatWorks: served_source_coverage is correct, complete and already served on the same route. source_health.sources (per-source lastFetched/ageHours) is also correct. source_runtime's partial/complete/failed source lists accurately describe the scraper run they cover.
rootCause: Same as W23-F003: `sites` is legacy browser-scraper metadata, and 19 of 21 sources now arrive as CSVs from scripts/fetch_*.py that never appear in it.
requiredRepair: Recompute source_health from served_source_coverage (with the registry as the expected set so missing_sources can actually be non-empty), or delete the three misleading fields and leave served_source_coverage as the single answer. Fix the stale "3-source" comment either way.

title: refit-hill-curves.yml opens a GitHub issue with no dedupe and no auto-close, alone among the six issue-opening workflows — a persistent condition mints one duplicate issue per week forever
claimUnderTest: The workflow's own comment at lines 180-185: "These issues close when a human runs `scripts/model_registry.py promote` + `apply`" — implying a bounded, self-clearing alert.
observed: The step is a bare `gh issue create --title "$TITLE" ... || gh issue create --title "$TITLE" ...` gated only on the refit driver's exit code. There is no `gh issue list --search` dedupe and `grep -c 'gh issue close' .github/workflows/refit-hill-curves.yml` returns 0. The workflow is weekly (cron '17 6 * * 2'), and the two titles are constant strings, so a challenger that keeps clearing the gate — or a regression that persists — produces one identical new issue every Tuesday and none of them ever closes automatically. Every one of the five sibling workflows that opens an issue does the idempotent thing: audit-rank-form-drift.yml, intel-refresh.yml, scheduled-refresh.yml, e2e.yml and audit-identity-matches.yml all search-then-comment and all carry a `gh issue close ... --reason completed` step on the green path. refit-hill-curves.yml is the only one with create-and-forget.

reproduction.command: for f in .github/workflows/*.yml; do c=$(grep -c 'gh issue create' "$f"); x=$(grep -c 'gh issue close' "$f"); s=$(grep -c 'issue list' "$f"); [ "$c" -gt 0 ] && echo "$(basename $f): create=$c close=$x dedupe_search=$s"; done
reproduction.expected: every workflow with create>0 also has close>0 and dedupe_search>0
reproduction.actual: refit-hill-curves.yml: create=2 close=0 dedupe_search=0 — the only outlier among six

numericProof.formula: duplicate issues per year for a persistent condition = cadence × (1 - has_dedupe) = 52 × 1

userImpact: No user-facing number. The operational cost is alert-channel decay: the issue tracker fills with identical "Hill refit: challenger cleared the held-out gate" issues, they stop being read, and the one week the alarm means something is indistinguishable from the fifty that did not. Since ADR-008 makes promotion an explicitly human step, this is the alert that is supposed to prompt that human.

priorFinding.note: PRIOR-A13-F14 reports 'No registry entry recorded since 2026-07-29 despite drift far above the threshold' and PRIOR-A07-F14 reports the refit audit trail stalling with 6 of 13 runs failing. Both are symptoms consistent with an alert nobody acts on; this finding names a specific mechanical reason the alert would be ignored. The duplicate-issue behavior itself is new to this shard and is provable from the workflow file alone (I cannot see the live issue tracker from this container, so the count of actual duplicates is unverified).

whatWorks: The gating logic is sound — exit code 1 (challenger cleared) and 3 (regression alarm) are distinguished with different titles and bodies, refit_report.txt is embedded, and the run URL is included. The `|| gh issue create` fallback correctly handles a missing `calibration` label. The deliberate decision not to auto-commit promoted constants (ADR-008) is correct and is respected here.
rootCause: The idempotent open-or-comment + auto-close pattern was written for scheduled-refresh.yml and copied into four later workflows; refit-hill-curves.yml predates or missed the copy.
requiredRepair: Port the sibling pattern: `gh issue list --search "in:title <TITLE>" --state open --json number` → comment if found, create if not; add an `if: success()` close step on the exit-code-0 path. audit-rank-form-drift.yml is the closest template and already matches on title rather than label specifically so it cannot reach across and close these.

title: scheduled-refresh.yml commits the data and dispatches the production deploy at steps 8-9, then runs the DLF-freshness assertion and both watchdogs at steps 10-13 — every guard except one is post-deploy, and none can roll back
claimUnderTest: scheduled-refresh.yml labels step 6 "Validate scrape sanity (pre-commit gate)" and describes the contract-coverage watchdog as catching "the silent registry / enrich / prime-timing regression that let ``otcffbSf`` be fetched + committed yet absent from the live board".
observed: Enumerating the job's steps in order: 6 Validate scrape sanity (the only true pre-commit gate), 7 retention prune, 8 Commit updated data, 9 Trigger deploy (`gh workflow run deploy.yml --ref main`), 10 Assert DLF freshness (`if: always()`), 11 Report freshness, 12 Staleness watchdog (`if: always()`), 13 Contract coverage watchdog (`if: always()`), 14 Alert on workflow failure (`if: failure()`). So three of the four data-quality guards evaluate AFTER the data is on main and the production deploy has been dispatched. When any of them goes red the workflow opens/updates a `stale-sources` tracking issue and stops — there is no revert, no re-deploy of the prior commit, and no call to deploy/rollback.sh anywhere in the workflow. The named regression (otcffbSf fetched and committed yet absent from the board) is by construction detected only after that exact commit has shipped. Compounding: step 9's `if: ${{ !cancelled() }}` means it runs even when step 8 was skipped by an upstream failure, in which case it inspects the PREVIOUS commit's message and can dispatch a deploy on a run whose sanity gate failed.

reproduction.command: .venv/bin/python -c "import yaml; d=yaml.safe_load(open('.github/workflows/scheduled-refresh.yml')); [print(f'{i:2d} {str(s.get(\"name\"))[:56]:56s} if={s.get(\"if\")}') for i,s in enumerate(d['jobs']['refresh']['steps'])]" && grep -c 'rollback\|git revert' .github/workflows/scheduled-refresh.yml
reproduction.expected: the coverage and freshness watchdogs ordered before 'Commit updated data', or a rollback path after them
reproduction.actual: watchdogs are steps 12 and 13; commit is step 8 and deploy dispatch is step 9; grep for rollback/revert returns 0

userImpact: A user on /rankings can be served a board missing an entire source for up to one full refresh cycle (2 h) plus however long a human takes to react to the tracking issue — the watchdog proves the board is wrong and the board stays live regardless. Because the failure mode is a MISSING source rather than a broken page, nothing in the UI signals it (see W23-F007/F008: the source-health surfaces cannot see 17 of 21 sources either).

priorFinding.note: Not in the prior index. Distinct from PRIOR-A07-F11 (docs describing a dead automation topology) — this is about live step ordering in a workflow that runs every two hours.

whatWorks: A great deal, and it should be said plainly: the watchdogs themselves are real and correctly wired. Both run under `if: always()` so a partial earlier failure still produces a red X; `set -Eeuo pipefail` with `tee` preserves watchdog_freshness.py's exit code through the pipe; the failure handler greps the teed log so the tracking issue names the actually-stale sources rather than a generic blurb; the issue is idempotent (search-then-comment) and auto-closes on a green run. validate_scrape_sanity.py IS a genuine pre-commit gate and does block the commit. This is a good detection system placed after the publish rather than before it.
rootCause: The commit+deploy steps were the original workflow; the watchdogs were appended later as detection, and the ordering was never revisited to make them gates.
requiredRepair: Move 'Contract coverage watchdog' and 'Assert DLF freshness' before 'Commit updated data' — the coverage watchdog builds the contract exactly as server._prime_latest_payload does and needs no committed state to run. Keep 'Staleness watchdog' where it is (it reports on stamps that step 5 writes) but add a revert-and-redeploy path when it fires, or gate step 9 on the watchdogs' success rather than on `!cancelled()`.
dependencies: W23-F003 (production's own in-process scrape loop runs neither watchdog, so the only coverage check anywhere is this CI one)

title: deploy/apply_hardening.sh is the sole installer for the 1-minute liveness watchdog, the 5-minute uptime probe and the 02:30 state backup, and no workflow, deploy script or timer ever invokes it
claimUnderTest: deploy/systemd/README.md:37 — "deploy/apply_hardening.sh installs/refreshes all of the above" — presented as part of the deployment story.
observed: deploy/deploy.sh and deploy/bootstrap-production.sh both invoke deploy/install-systemd-service.sh, which renders 12 of the 13 timer templates under deploy/systemd/ plus the riskit-backup pair. It does NOT touch dynasty-healthcheck.{service,timer}, riskit-state-backup.{service,timer} or riskit-uptime.{service,timer} — those three are installed only by apply_hardening.sh, whose sole documented invocation is a hand-typed `sudo bash deploy/apply_hardening.sh` (its own header, line 19). A repo-wide grep for `apply_hardening` outside docs and its own body returns zero callers. Consequences if the manual step was ever missed or the host was rebuilt: the 1-minute backend liveness watchdog does not restart a hung service, the 5-minute external uptime probe never runs, and the 02:30 state backup does not happen. The running instance corroborates the shape of this: /api/uptime returns {"enabled": false, "last_check": null}. (That specific value is container state and is not itself the finding — the finding is that nothing in automation guarantees these three units exist on a deployed host.)

reproduction.command: grep -rn 'apply_hardening' --include='*.sh' --include='*.yml' . | grep -v '\.venv\|node_modules\|apply_hardening.sh:' ; echo "callers above (empty = none)"; for u in dynasty-healthcheck riskit-state-backup riskit-uptime; do echo "$u in install-systemd-service.sh: $(grep -c $u deploy/install-systemd-service.sh)"; done
reproduction.expected: at least one automated caller, or these three installed by install-systemd-service.sh
reproduction.actual: no callers outside docs; dynasty-healthcheck 0, riskit-state-backup 0, riskit-uptime 0 in install-systemd-service.sh

userImpact: If the backend hangs, nothing restarts it and nothing pages anyone — the site is down until a human notices. If the host is rebuilt from the documented deploy path alone, user_kv and session_store have no nightly backup, so a disk loss takes every user's saved team, watchlist and alert rules with it.

priorFinding.note: Independently reproduced by cross-referencing all 19 timer units against the two installers. Adds the precise split: install-systemd-service.sh renders 12 of 13 deploy/systemd templates plus riskit-backup, and the three orphans live in deploy/systemd (healthcheck), deploy/monitoring and deploy/backup.

whatWorks: apply_hardening.sh itself is well-built — idempotent, has a --dry-run, and enables the timers it installs. install-systemd-service.sh's coverage of the other 12 templates is thorough and guarded (it checks for both service and timer templates and for required secrets before installing). Both scripts do their job; nothing joins them.
rootCause: Two installer scripts grew independently — one for app units on every deploy, one for host-hardening units as a one-off — and the hardening set was never folded into the recurring path.
requiredRepair: Either call apply_hardening.sh from deploy.sh (it is already idempotent, so this is safe) or move the three unit pairs into install-systemd-service.sh's render loop. Add a post-deploy assertion in deploy/verify-deploy.sh that `systemctl is-enabled` returns enabled for all three.

title: ops_alerts.py's docstring advertises six alert conditions; the module implements four — the signal-alert-cron-staleness and SQLite-integrity checks do not exist
claimUnderTest: src/api/ops_alerts.py lines 6-11 list six conditions, including "Signal-alert cron hasn't run in > 36h (expected every 12h)" and "Session-store SQLite integrity check fails".
observed: check_and_alert() calls exactly four checks: _check_scrape_rate, _check_circuit_breakers, _check_contract_health, _check_data_freshness. There is no function for cron staleness and none for SQLite integrity, and no other module supplies them to this path. The docstring's parenthetical is also wrong about cadence: deploy/systemd/dynasty-signal-alerts.timer.template is `OnCalendar=*-*-* 15:00:00 UTC`, i.e. once daily, not every 12 h — so a self-check written to the advertised spec would have been miscalibrated anyway. With W23-F001, the live check count is effectively three.

reproduction.command: grep -n 'def _check' src/api/ops_alerts.py; sed -n '221,233p' src/api/ops_alerts.py; grep OnCalendar deploy/systemd/dynasty-signal-alerts.timer.template
reproduction.actual: four _check_* functions defined and invoked; OnCalendar=*-*-* 15:00:00 UTC (daily, not 12-hourly)

userImpact: Nobody reads this docstring at runtime. The risk is a maintainer trusting it: the signal-alert cron can stop firing entirely — taking the custom-alert, BDVM-signal, ops-alert and source-staleness sweeps with it, since all four piggyback on that one endpoint — and nothing is watching the watcher.

priorFinding.note: Confirmed exactly, and extended: the docstring's '(expected every 12h)' also contradicts the shipped timer, which is daily at 15:00 UTC — so both the check and its stated threshold are wrong.

whatWorks: The four implemented checks are correctly structured, the 4-hour cooldown keyed in user_kv under _system_ops_alerts works, and recovery alerts fire once on clear. check_and_alert never raises, as advertised.
rootCause: The docstring was written as a plan for six checks; four were built.
requiredRepair: Either implement the two missing checks (cron staleness is easy — compare now() against the last signal-alert sweep timestamp already stored in user_kv) or delete the two bullets. Fix the 12h → daily discrepancy in the same edit.

title: The FFPC Sharp crawl ships as two byte-identical timer templates in two directories with two different installers and the same 05:20 UTC schedule
claimUnderTest: Implicit: one crawl, one schedule, one unit.
observed: `diff deploy/systemd/dynasty-ffpc-sharp.timer.template deploy/ffpc-systemd/chase-upside-ffpc-sharp.timer.template` returns no differences — both are OnCalendar=*-*-* 05:20:00 UTC with RandomizedDelaySec=900. They are installed under different unit names by different scripts (install-systemd-service.sh renders the dynasty-* pair; install-ffpc-sharp-service.sh renders the chase-upside-* pair, which install-systemd-service.sh never references). Both service templates invoke scripts/crawl_ffpc_sharp.py. On a host where both installers have been run, the FFPC crawl fires twice within the same 15-minute randomized window every day, doubling outbound requests to FFPC and racing two writers into the same platform ledger.

reproduction.command: diff deploy/systemd/dynasty-ffpc-sharp.timer.template deploy/ffpc-systemd/chase-upside-ffpc-sharp.timer.template && echo IDENTICAL; grep -l crawl_ffpc_sharp deploy/systemd/*.template deploy/ffpc-systemd/*.template; grep -c 'chase-upside-ffpc-sharp' deploy/install-systemd-service.sh
reproduction.actual: IDENTICAL; both service templates invoke crawl_ffpc_sharp.py; install-systemd-service.sh references the chase-upside name 0 times (separate installer)

numericProof.formula: daily invocations = number of installed timers

userImpact: None visible to a user unless the double crawl trips FFPC rate limiting or the concurrent ledger writes corrupt observation counts, either of which would surface as a thinner or wrong Sharp Tracker board.

priorFinding.note: Confirmed by byte-identical diff. Confidence is medium rather than high on the IMPACT half only: I cannot observe the production host, so whether both installers have actually been run there is unverifiable from this container. The duplication in the repo is certain.

whatWorks: Each pair on its own is well-formed — explicit UTC, randomized delay, Persistent=true.
rootCause: The FFPC crawl was prototyped with its own installer under a product-branded unit name and later folded into the standard dynasty-* naming, without deleting the prototype.
requiredRepair: Delete deploy/ffpc-systemd/ and deploy/install-ffpc-sharp-service.sh, and add a `systemctl disable --now chase-upside-ffpc-sharp.timer` to the deploy path so an already-installed duplicate is cleaned up rather than silently left running.

title: dynasty-custom-alerts.timer's systemd Description says "Hourly custom-alert sweep" while its OnCalendar fires every two hours
observed: `OnCalendar=*-*-* 0/2:13:00 UTC` — every two hours at :13, with RandomizedDelaySec=180. The body comment two lines below the Description correctly says "Fire every two hours", so the file contradicts itself. Description is the string systemd surfaces in `systemctl list-timers` and `systemctl status`, which is exactly where an operator checks a schedule.
userImpact: A user's price-crossing alert can arrive up to ~2 h after the crossing rather than the ~1 h the unit name implies to whoever tuned it. The operator-facing harm is larger than the user-facing one: `systemctl list-timers` lies about the cadence.

priorFinding.note: Confirmed verbatim from the template. Noting additionally that the file's own inline comment already states the correct interval, so this is a stale Description rather than a disagreement about intent.

whatWorks: The schedule itself is deliberate and well-reasoned (the inline comment ties the 2 h cadence to the scrape interval and to custom_alerts.py's 24 h per-rule cooldown), and the explicit UTC suffix is correct and better than most systemd units in the wild.
rootCause: The timer was originally hourly; the interval was changed and the Description was not.

title: 28 of 89 scripts/ entrypoints have no scheduler and no production caller, including five validators whose whole purpose is to be a guard that runs
claimUnderTest: Implicit: scripts/ is the pipeline's helper layer, so a script there is part of the pipeline.
observed: Scanning 1,358 non-vendored files for `scripts/<name>` and `scripts.<module>` invocation forms: 39 of 89 top-level scripts are reachable from a workflow, a systemd unit template, a deploy script, a Makefile/Jenkinsfile/.bat, another script, or src/. 28 have no such reference at all (3 more are referenced only by tests). Most are legitimately one-off research (backtest_*, measure_*), and calling those dead would be wrong. The ones that matter are the five VALIDATORS and board-guards: validate_sharp_roster_percentage.py, validate_va_v2.py, validate_scoring_fit.py, board_invariance_hash.py and golden_board.py. A validator that no scheduler runs and no gate calls is indistinguishable from a validator that does not exist — the specific pattern CLAUDE.md's rule 6 asks to be called out. Two scripts also reference siblings that are not in scripts/ at all (measure_engine_value_divergence.py is reached only from scripts/audit/finder_migration_snapshot.py; persist_nfl_actuals.py only from scripts/audit/measure_usage_signal_rate.py), so their reachability runs through the audit subtree rather than the pipeline.

reproduction.command: awk -F, 'NR>1 && $2=="none" && ($5=="NOTHING"||$5=="TESTS ONLY")' docs/master-site-audit/evidence/W23/schedule-map.csv | cut -d, -f1 | wc -l; grep -E '^scripts/(validate_|board_invariance|golden_board)' docs/master-site-audit/evidence/W23/schedule-map.csv | cut -d, -f1,2,5
reproduction.expected: validators either scheduled or invoked by a gate
reproduction.actual: 28 unreferenced; validate_sharp_roster_percentage.py / validate_va_v2.py / validate_scoring_fit.py / board_invariance_hash.py / golden_board.py all show scheduled_by=none, read_by=NOTHING

userImpact: Indirect. The board-invariance hash and golden-board comparison are precisely the tools that would catch an unintended repricing between refits, and neither runs, so an unintended board shift reaches /rankings with no automated tripwire.

priorFinding.note: PRIOR-A13-F07 makes the same shape of claim about the tier-threshold fitter specifically ('no fitter that can run'). This finding generalizes it across scripts/ with a full census. Confidence is medium because the invocation scan is a static text search: a script invoked via a shell variable, a fully dynamic path, or an operator runbook outside the repo would be misclassified as dead. The five validators were each spot-checked by hand.

whatWorks: The 39 reachable scripts are properly wired — the 14 fetch_* scripts to scheduled-refresh.yml, the four sharp crawlers to their timer templates, refresh_playerctx/refresh_reception_depth/refresh_bdvm_projections/snapshot_consensus_edge to systemd templates, and check_env.py to seven workflows. The full mapping is in schedule-map.csv.
rootCause: scripts/ mixes three populations with no naming or directory separation: scheduled production jobs, human-invoked research, and validators that were written for a gate that was never wired.
requiredRepair: Wire the five validators to something (board_invariance_hash + golden_board belong in scheduled-refresh.yml next to validate_scrape_sanity.py; validate_sharp_roster_percentage belongs after the sharp-rosters timer), or move them to scripts/audit/ alongside the other explicitly-manual tooling so the distinction is visible.

title: VERIFIED NEGATIVE — all 22 workflow files parse cleanly and none contains a duplicate mapping key, so no workflow is silently unrunnable for that reason
claimUnderTest: The audit brief's hypothesis: "do any workflows fail to PARSE (a YAML duplicate-key class error would stop a workflow from ever running)?"
observed: All 22 files load under yaml.SafeLoader without error. Loaded again under a custom constructor that raises on any repeated key in any mapping at any depth, all 22 still load clean. There is no duplicate-key defect and no parse defect in .github/workflows/. Recording this because a verified negative is a result: the reason four Sharp workflows never reach their verdict is the gitignore interaction in W23-F004, not a parse failure, and future readers should not re-litigate the YAML.
userImpact: None — this is a negative result confirming the CI definitions are structurally sound.

priorFinding.note: No prior finding claims a parse error; this closes the hypothesis explicitly.

whatWorks: All 22 workflow definitions. Schedules extracted cleanly for all 14 cron-driven workflows and all 19 systemd timer units — see schedule-map.csv.

title: There is no human review layer: nothing in the UI can approve, suppress, annotate, re-run, diff or roll back a single suspicious output — the pipeline publishes and the pages render whatever it produced
claimUnderTest: frontend/app/admin/page.jsx lines 1-15 — "operator dashboard for flipping feature flags, running one-off admin actions ... the infrastructure of 'one place for all admin levers' is the point."
observed: Full inventory of every operator lever that exists. /admin exposes exactly three actions (Flush NFL data cache, Migrate signal state, Force-logout all sessions) plus a guest-pass panel; ServerStatusPanel adds one more, POST /api/scrape. The docstring's headline claim — "flipping feature flags" — is false: the page renders featureFlags read-only and there is no write endpoint for a flag anywhere in server.py (flags are env vars read once per process; CLAUDE.md itself says "Rollback: RISKIT_FEATURE_BDVM_ENGINE=0 and restart ... there is no runtime toggle"). Against the four capabilities the brief asks about: APPROVE/SUPPRESS — absent; the only quarantine in the product is pipeline-computed (row.quarantined, rendered dimmed on /rankings) and there is no route or control to quarantine, unquarantine or exempt a row by hand. ANNOTATE — absent; no note, reason or provenance field is writable on any player, source or value. RE-RUN — present but all-or-nothing: POST /api/scrape re-runs the entire scrape; there is no per-source or per-player recompute. COMPARE VERSIONS — absent from the UI; scripts/board_diff.py and scripts/golden_board.py exist and are exactly the right tools, and per W23-F015 neither has a scheduler or a caller, let alone a page. ROLL BACK A MODEL — CLI only: scripts/model_registry.py promote/apply is referenced from server.py and the frontend zero times. ROLL BACK A DEPLOY — CLI only: deploy/rollback.sh, invoked by no workflow. The nearest thing to a human gate in the whole system is ADR-008's rule that Hill-curve constants move only by a human running two CLI commands — a genuine gate, but one that lives entirely outside the product. Everything a user reads on /rankings, /trade and /draft is whatever the last pipeline run produced, with no interposed approval and no way to intervene short of shell access to the host.

reproduction.command: grep -n 'runAction(' frontend/app/admin/page.jsx; grep -n '"/api/scrape"' frontend/components/admin/ServerStatusPanel.jsx; grep -n '"/api/admin' server.py; grep -rniE 'approve|suppress|annotat|rollback|override' frontend/app/admin/ | wc -l; grep -rn 'model_registry' server.py frontend/app frontend/components | wc -l
reproduction.actual: 3 runAction calls + 1 scrape trigger; 6 /api/admin routes (flush, force-logout, guest-pass x3, signal-state migrate); 0 approve/suppress/annotate/rollback matches under frontend/app/admin/; 0 references to model_registry from server or UI

numericProof.formula: UI coverage = present_in_ui / capabilities; the one present (re-run) is whole-pipeline only, not per-output

userImpact: When the pipeline emits a wrong value — and this shard alone documents three ways it can do so unnoticed (W23-F003 promotes a near-total-loss board, W23-F006 hides its age, W23-F010 ships it before the coverage watchdog runs) — a user sees that number on /rankings and trades on it. The operator's only options are re-run the entire scrape and hope, or SSH to the host. There is no way to suppress one bad row, annotate it as suspect, or revert the board to the previous snapshot.

priorFinding.note: PRIOR-A06-F08 says /admin renders to any signed-in user because its load-time gate is a public endpoint — an access-control finding about the page that exists. This is the orthogonal question the brief asks: what the page can DO. Confirmed independently that the mutating routes are separately gated (POST /api/admin/* returns 403 for the non-allowlisted e2e-test-user, per AUDIT_PROTOCOL's note), so the exposure is of the read-only view; the capability gap recorded here is unaffected either way.

whatWorks: What exists is honest about itself. The three admin actions are real, confirmation-gated, and write a visible in-session action log with HTTP status and response body. The guest-pass panel supports issue and revoke. ServerStatusPanel's scrape trigger works. /tools/ros-data-health and /tools/trade-coverage are genuine read-only diagnostics. And the deliberate human-in-the-loop design for Hill-curve promotion (ADR-008) is a real gate that the refit workflow respects — it just isn't reachable from the product.
rootCause: The system was built as an automated pipeline with observability bolted on; the operator surfaces answer "what happened" and were never extended to "and let me do something about this specific thing". There is no persistence layer for per-asset operator state (no overrides table, no annotations, no approval status), so no UI could be built without one.
requiredRepair: Smallest useful increment, in order: (1) a per-row operator suppression stored in user_kv or a new table, honored by the materializer the same way row.quarantined already is — this alone gives a way to pull one bad value; (2) surface scripts/board_diff.py as a /tools/board-diff page comparing the live contract to the previous snapshot, which makes 'is this run suspicious' answerable before acting; (3) a documented one-command board rollback (re-prime from the previous data/dynasty_data_*.json) exposed on /admin. Approve/annotate can wait; suppress and diff are what the failure modes in this shard actually call for.
